passages.text: The Merton problem is the well-known stochastic control problem of choosing consumption over time, as well as an investment mix, to maximize expected constant relative risk aversion utility of consumption. Merton formulated the problem and provided an analytical solution in 1970; since then a number of extensions of the original formulation have been solved. In this note we identify a certainty equivalent problem, i.e., a deterministic optimal control problem with the same optimal value function and optimal policy, for the base Merton problem, as well as a number of extensions. When time is discretized, the certainty equivalent problem becomes a second-order cone program, readily formulated and solved using domain specific languages for convex optimization. This makes it a good starting point for model predictive control, a policy that can handle extensions that are either too cumbersome or impossible to handle exactly using standard dynamic programming methods.

passages.text: We revisit Merton’s seminal 1970 formulation (and solution) of the consumption and investment decisions of an individual investor. We present a formulation of Merton’s problem as a deterministic convex optimal control problem, and in particular, a SOCP when time is discretized. Even though the Merton problem was first solved more than 50 years ago, its reformulation as a deterministic convex optimization problem provides fresh insight into the solution of the stochastic problem that may be useful for formulating other multiperiod investment problems as convex optimization problems.

passages.text: The second and perhaps more significant advantage is that the certainty equivalent problem can be used as a starting point for further extensions of the Merton problem, for which no closed-form solutions are known. In this case, the certainty equivalence property is lost, and solving the deterministic problem no longer solves the corresponding stochastic problem exactly. We can, however, still use model predictive control, a method that involves online convex optimization, to develop a policy that handles the extension. MPC policies are simple, easy to implement, fully interpretable, and have excellent (if not always optimal) practical performance.

passages.text: Merton’s problem. Merton’s consumption–investment problem dates back to his original 1970 paper. Many extensions to the basic Merton problem exist, some of which were covered in Merton’s original paper. These include deterministic income and general HARA utility. Most proposed extensions do not have a closed-form solution, but some that do include uncertain mortality, life insurance, and annuities, first addressed by Rice. Some extensions for the specific case of quadratic utility are handled in the work of Bogle and Candele. We note that many of these extensions individually lead to complicated solutions, and deriving the optimal policy when several extensions are combined may be very inconvenient for a practical implementation.

passages.text: Certainty equivalence. Rarely, stochastic control problems have a certainty equivalent formulation, that is, a deterministic optimal control problem with the same optimal policy. The most famous example is the linear quadratic regulator problem, in which the dynamics are affine, driven by additive noise, and the stage costs are convex quadratic. In this case, the certainty equivalent problem is obtained by simply ignoring the stochastic noise term. Many extensions to linear quadratic control also have a certainty equivalent reformulation. Examples include the linear quadratic Gaussian problem, in which the state is imperfectly observed, and linear exponential quadratic regulator problem, which uses a risk-sensitive cost function. Our certainty equivalent formulation is similar to linear exponential quadratic regulator in that the uncertain quantity is adversarial. For the Merton problem, the uncertain quantity is the investment returns.

passages.text: Model predictive control. In model predictive control, unknown values of future parameters are replaced with estimates or forecasts over a planning horizon extending from the current time to some time in the future, resulting in a deterministic optimal control problem. This problem is solved, with the result intrepretable as a plan of action over the planning horizon. The MPC policy simply uses the current or first value in the plan of action. This planning is repeated when updated forecasts are available, using the updated forecasts and current state. When applied in the context of stochastic control, MPC policies are not optimal in general, but often exhibit excellent practical performance, and are widely used in several application areas. MPC is discussed in detail in BBM17 and KH06. In Boy+14, the authors use a computational bound to show that MPC is nearly optimal for some stochastic control problems in finance.

passages.text: Multi-period portfolio optimization. It is instructive to compare our certainty equivalent problem to popular formulations of multi-period portfolio allocation. There are two features present in our certainty equivalent problem that we do not see in practical multiperiod portfolio construction problems in the literature: First, the risk term, which is quadratic in the dollar-valued asset allocation vector x t, is normalized by the total wealth w t, which is also a decision variable. This risk term is jointly convex in x t and w t, and is in fact SOCP representable. With this normalization, risk preferences are consistent even as the wealth w t changes over the investment horizon.

2 The Merton Problem

In this section we discuss the Merton problem and its solution. To keep the proofs concise, we consider the most basic form of this problem; extensions are considered later. Our formulation is in continuous time and relies on stochastic calculus. However, to maintain both brevity and accessibility, we are cavalier about the technical details, with the assumption that a sophisticated reader can fill in the gaps, or consult other references.

Equation 9 says to maximize the sum of two terms. The first term is beta divided by gamma, multiplied by wealth at time T raised to the power of gamma. The second term is the integral from 0 to T of consumption at time t raised to the power of gamma, then divided by gamma. This is subject to several constraints. First, the time derivative of wealth, w dot t, is less than or equal to the product of the transpose of the mean return vector mu and the dollar allocation x t, minus consumption c t, plus a risk term. This risk term is computed as follows: first subtract 1 from gamma, then multiply that by the product of x t transpose, the covariance matrix sigma, and x t, then divide that result by 2, and finally divide by wealth w t. This holds for t in the interval from 0 to T. Second, the ratio of x t to w t must be in the set Theta for t in the interval from 0 to T. Third, wealth at time 0 equals the initial wealth w init.

The variables are the consumption c t, a function from the interval 0 to T to the positive real numbers; wealth w t, a function from the interval 0 to T to the positive real numbers; and x t, a function from the interval 0 to T to the n dimensional real space, which is the dollar-valued allocation of wealth to each asset. In the notation of section 2, we have x t equals w t times theta t, and theta t equals x t divided by w t. Note that the constraint x t divided by w t is in Theta implies that the sum of the elements of x t equals w t, i.e., the total wealth is the sum of the dollar-valued asset allocations.

passages.text: Annuities and life insurance: This extension is due to Rice. Continuing with the previous extension, we allow the investor to purchase life insurance. The premium is l t, which the investor can choose, and the payout of the plan is lambda t times l t, where lambda t is greater than or equal to zero and represents the payout-to-premium ratio at time t. When l t is less than zero, we interpret this as an annuity. In particular, at time t, the investor has negative l t in the annuity account, which is lost on death, in return for an additional return of negative lambda t times l t. The actuarially fair value of lambda t is p t divided by s t, which is called the force of mortality. If lambda t is greater than p t divided by s t, then life insurance is favorable and annuities are unfavorable; if lambda t is less than p t divided by s t, the reverse is true.

passages.text: Model predictive control is a technique for stochastic control problems that leverages a deterministic approximation of the stochastic problem. To evaluate an MPC policy, we first solve this deterministic problem to obtain a planned trajectory for the state and control input over the planning horizon. We then implement only the first control input in this plan, and the rest of the planned trajectory is discarded. To obtain future control inputs, the policy is evaluated again, which requires solving a new deterministic problem.

passages.text: In the context of the Merton problem, the certainty equivalent problem is used as a basis for a simple model predictive control policy. We first define this policy when t equals 0, with initial wealth w 0. We start by solving the deterministic control problem 9 to obtain the optimal trajectories c t and theta t. The MPC policy then takes the initial consumption and allocation as the values at time 0. To define the MPC policy for t between 0 and T, we first form a new instance of problem 9, which is defined over the interval from t to T and has initial wealth w t. Once again we solve the deterministic optimal control problem 9, to obtain optimal c tau and theta tau over the interval tau from t to T. We then take the MPC policy at time t to be the consumption and allocation values at that time. Evaluating the MPC policy therefore always requires solving a deterministic optimal control problem of the form 9.

passages.text: The discretized problem is implemented as follows: we define variables for wealth over K plus one time steps, asset allocations for n assets over K plus one time steps, and consumption over K time steps. We compute the Cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix Sigma. The objective is to maximize the sum of the discounted bequest utility, which is beta divided by gamma times wealth at the final step raised to the power of gamma, and the integrated consumption utility, which is h divided by gamma times the sum of consumption raised to the power of gamma. The constraints specify that wealth equals the sum of asset allocations at each step, and that initial wealth equals w init. For each time step k, the change in wealth divided by h is less than or equal to the product of the mean return vector mu and the asset allocations, minus consumption, plus a risk penalty. This penalty is the quantity gamma minus one divided by two, multiplied by the quadratic-over-linear function of the product of the Cholesky factor and the asset allocations, divided by wealth. Finally, we define the problem to maximize the utility U subject to these constraints and solve it.

```
w = Variable (K+1)
x = Variable (n, K+1)
c = Variable (K)
Sigma_half = numpy.linalg.cholesky (Sigma)
U = beta/gamma * power(w[K], gamma) + h/gamma * sum(power(c,
   gamma))
constr = [w == sum(x, axis=0), w[0] == w_init]
for k in range(K):
    constr += [diff(w[k+1] - w[k])/h <= mu @ x[:, k] - c[k] +
       (gamma - 1)/2 * quad_over_lin(Sigma_half @ x[:, k], w[k
       ])]
]
problem = Problem(Maximize (U), constr)
problem .solve()
```

passages.text: To give some idea of the speed at which current solvers can solve the discretized problem and its extensions, consider a problem with 500 assets, 50 periods, and a covariance matrix given as a typical factor model with 25 factors. This problem has more than 100,000 optimization variables. With just a small modification of the code given in listing 1 to exploit the low rank plus diagonal structure of the covariance matrix, the open-source solver ECOS solves the problem in around two seconds, on a single thread.
